Five bandits held up a Winona mail
wagon about 4:30 am. today, tied
the messengers hands and feet with
wire and gagged him and then after
selecting the four registered mail
pouches out of between so and SC
bags. headed toward the Twin Cities
in an automobile.


The messenger, Henry Williams.
was on his way from the Chicago,
Milwaukee G. St. Paul depot to the
post office. When about three blocks
from the depot five men intercepted
him, led him into an alley and
warned him against. any ourcry and
told him to take orders"


While two men covered the mes
senger with guns, one tied him with
wire. He was then forced to lie on
the ground, face downward. Mean
while. the two others were scattering
the mail bags hurriedly about the
ground searching for registered
pouches.


With the four registered mail
pouches the bandits fed in an auto
mobile. Before departing they told
Williams that he should not move
for half hour.


Postmaster E. B. Hicks said that
the monetary value of the stolen
mail could not be estimated at pres
ent, but, he doubted that the four
pouches contained any great sum.


The robbery was discovered when
Burlington railroad employe, be-
coming alarmed at his failure to find
the morning mail on his arrival for
work, found Williams in the alley
lying beside the mail wagon.

pigeonholed, however, for the globe

was to determine the possibilities of
running commercial or mail routes
from the United States through Gem
trail America and thus bring South
america closer to the business cen
ters of the United States by many
days if not weeks.

NEW YORK, May 1.-May day eve
was marked here by police raids on
10 meetings of Communists, Socialists
and alleged anarchists, at which all
the participants were driven into the
street. Only two arrests We're made
during the day and those were young
men handing out pamphlets of a
reputedly melting nature to school
children.


The most important raid of the
night was at the Manhattan headquar-
ters of the Workers Party of Amer
lea. where all members, including
classes OF the Workers League and
the Trade Union Educational League,
were driven into the street. Desks
were broken open and literature con-
fiScated.


There was no violence in any of the
raids. At the Bronx headquarters of
the Workers Party, where police
found three separate meetings being
conducted in three separate languages,
samples of literature were taken and
the names and addresses of leaders OBJ
tained after which the meetings We're
permitted 10 continue. Other meet
ings, however were broken up, the
members being given their choice of
quitting the hall or being thrown out.
In every case they elected to quit the
hall.


Foster Scores Raiders.


William 4. Foster, leader of the
1919 steel strike, who was at the Man
haitian headquarters of the Workers
Party when this place was raided last
night, demanded that the raiders show
their search warrants for breaking
into the desks and their authority for
ordering those present out into the
streets.


Foster said after the meeting that
he would make formal complaint with
Police Commissioner Enright.


Police today are guarding all public
buildings and the homes of all noted
men and public officials. All special
squads are on duty, and orders have
been sent out from headquarters for
extreme police vigilance in every part
of the city.

HOOKWORMS are small worms
III about one.half inch long ana
Of about the thickness of a coarse
thread: in fact, they look like
short nieces of thread. They are
incapable of reproducing them
selves in the human body. They
do however, lay eggs which are
discharged with the intestinal con-
tents and when these eggs fall
unon moist, shady, warm ground
thew soon develop into small
larvae. When they come in con-
tact with the bare skin they at
fach themselves to it. Persons
Who 90 barefooted are likely to
contract the disease.


Once the larvae have attached
themselves to the skin they soon
nenetrate II and fino their way
into the lymphatics, whence they
are carried into the heart. From
the heart thew pass into the lungs
There they penetrate the little air
sacs and are breathed up into
the throat and then swallowed.


Finally they find their way into
the small intestine, where they
lodge themselves by means Of
hooks in their mouths. hence the
name "hookworm." These para
sites feed from sucking blood
from the intestines, thus impover-
ishing their victim and gradually
producing anaemia.

Iuther's much -trumpeted onslaught
on the high cost of living seems likely
to meet the fate of most attempts to
tamper with economic laws--it prob
ably will not influence prices, but may
result in the disappearance OF goods
and leave the chancellor with dl-
minished prestige.


The governments action was upder-
taken Immediately after the Reich
stag's conservative majority passed
the new tariff bill and the new tax
schedule. The former increases the
profits of the big land owners and the
iudustrialists. The latter reduced their
taxes without an equivalent Tightening
of the burdens on the poorer strata.


Moreover, the infinitely patient Ger
man workers were beginning to
grumble. Their net wages by and
large throughout Germany run from
81 TO 81 day. while the cost of living
assuming similar consumption is about
equal TO the American figures. That
the German masses exist at all is due
To their incredibly low living stand
ards.


Therefore. the cabinet undertook to
undo the bad impression caused by



,tackinc the price cartels. These as
Sociations of merchants and producers
cover Germany and often extend to
other countries. Their aim is to sup
press competition, control internal
markets and raise prices to the
maximum.


The cabinet declares it will force
the CartelS 10 loosen or at least relax
their strangle-h hold. The Cartels have
- ,l,at-S iYo nar-

reductions. The question arose, who
was getting the money. Official price
lists seemed to show that the retailers
We're making colossal profits. 1t was
stated butchers often made 40 per
cent and more.


The Retailers Association protested
and declared that no possibility of
price reductions existed so long as
the wholesalers refused TO relax their
prices. Thereupon, the officials re-
considered the question and found

for the intolerable living costs.


Prompt Denial Follows.

bN the til III IdN anu tHt Iie" ldA

Therefore. the struggle has become

The several social strata


L
patience. Several strikes have re-
suited. and others are threatened.

over Germany have risen perhaps )
per cent but meanwhile the cos of
living has about doubled. and the
prices of fOodstuffs are soaring.

unions received partial satisfaction.
notably the building trades and the

randa first from the employers. then

opportunity to earn some money for

reached Il point that threatens to en-

have already filed their applications
for the extra. work his permanent
force would not only have their
Christmas day free, but also all the
rest of the year.


He explained, however, that selec-
tions of men to augment the regular
force this Christmas have already
been made from the mass Of applica-
tions filed many weeks ago, and last
minute opportunities for employment
are useless. He has asked that fur
ther solicitations for this work be
discontinued.

PARIS, Sept. 24.-General Game
lin has led French forces into
Sueida, relieving the French gar
rison there which has been be-
sieged for more than month, ac-
cording to dispatches today from
Syria.


For several weeks the rebellious
Djebel Druses have been at the
gate of Sueida threatening to wipe
out the French garrison at any
moment. During the past week
advancing French troops have been
registering successes against the
Druses, finally penetrating their
lines and administering a severe
defeat to them and entering Sueida
to relieve the besieged garrison.


The French foreign office an
nounced today that it had received
dispatches from Damascus stating
that General Gamelin with 500
soldiers entered Sueida last night,
carrying in supplies to the besieged
garrison. The report added that
the Druses have been driven back,
and their. siege Of Sueida is def
nitely broken.

BOSTON, August 13.-George H.
Curtis of the West Roxbury district
and his wife Mary are dead and two
of their three children are believed to
be dying at the City Hospital of bullet
wounds in the head. A daughter.
Dorothy, the only member of the fam
lily who escaped injury, told the police
her mother shot the others early to-
day in a fit of depression and COM
mitted suicide.


George H. Curtis, jr., 20, and Mar
jorie, Z, were shot while they slept,
their sister said. Dorothy reported
that she escaped because she slept on
an upper floor and spent some time in
dressing after her mother called her,
shortly after 6 o'clock. Before she
had finished dressing she heard four
shots. When she reached the lower
floor she found both her parents dead
and her brother and sister wounded.


Several months ago, the police were
told, Mrs. Curtis suffered a stroke.
which resulted in partial paralysis of
the left side of her body. Since that
time she had BEEN depressed and had
acted strangely, her daughter said.

The United States Marine Corps
is now considering the advisabiHty
of adopting the roll collar in place
of the standing collar that has
characterized the uniform for
many years.


For several years officers of the
Navy have been wearing the roll
collar Only recently Secretary of
War Davis, after having permitted
it's adoption by the Air Service,
announced that hereafter the roll
collar will be standard for the en-
tire Army.


Normally the Marine Corps sets
the pace and the recruiting slogans
emphasize the fact that the ma
rines are always first on the spot,
but in this instance they seem to
have been asleep at the switch.


Throughout the corps both Off
GERS and enlisted men already are
asking when they can substitute
the roll for the tight collar. This
is especially true of men on duty
in the tropics. The much greater
comfort of the roll collar Is con-
ceded even by its critics.

Armed bandits today held up and
robbed the paymaster Of the wood
mill here and escaped with a box
containing pay envelopes holding
several thousand dollars.


The robbery was staged in the
card room Of the mill. AS the pay
master, George Alexander, and his
guard entered the room they were
met with a leveled gun and the
money seized.


Firing two shots, neither of which
took effect, the bandit raced
through another door, guarded by
an accomplice and disappeared.
Police and mill officials do not know
whether the men left the building
or are hiding inside the six-story
mill structure.

been congested with five classes ever

lack Of heat. Armstrong; students

order to consider whether rates on
anthracite coal produced in Virginia

consuming territory and whether
through and Joint rates from southern

low volatile coal districts to combine
IN the making of joint rates that
would allow the movement of the
anti. acite substitute. These new and

10. The orders today indicated that
the commission saw a possibility of
enlarging their scope and of getting
into the Atlantic Coast consuming ter
ritotry additional coal which may be
needed to substitute for the anthracite
supply.


The Virginia anthracite deposits
have hitherto been marketed in a
limited territory. The new West Vir-
ginia producing territory to which
the commission will consider estab-
lishment of lower joint rates includes
points in Kanawha, Coal River. New
River, Pocahontas and Tug River dis
tricts. The object of the hearing will
be to determine whether the railroad
rates now effective from these points
may not be modified and lowered bv

campaign against all foreigners.


Strenuous efforts were made to
extend the general strike to all es.
sential services, particularly utilities,

plies and starving out the foreign
population.

with fresh reinforce1nents of

ice have been halted. Provisions

ants who heretofore have been loyal

appeals, through which runs red

The famous pigeon-bIood rubies
of Burma. the finest of which, since
the time of Akbar the Great, have
come from the Mogok ruby mines,
which lie ninety miles north Of
Mandalay in the heart of the Bur-
mese Peninsula, are now mined
electrically.


Almost since the time when "the
memory of man runneth not to the
contrary" naked brown workmen
have dug the soil of this mine by
hand and carried it in baskets to
the sorting sheds. Here other coolies
have carefully conabed the earth
with their nimble fingers in search
of precious Burmese rubies. Now
all this. is changed, for. near the
Mogok mines runs the Yeni-Choung
river, which has been harnessed "A
series of turbines at this hydro
electric development produces 900
horsepower of electrical energy,
which is transmitted through the
jungles to the mines. Here, with
electrification, small trucks hauled
by endless belts, carry the ruby
bearing earth to the sorting sheds.
Electric pumps keeps the mines
dry and electric motors operate
the various pieces of machinery all
the way from the biggest to the
tiny wheels upon which the rubies
are cut and polished.


Electricity is also used for light
ing not only the bungalows where
live the British managers and the
Eurasian mine staff, but also for
the powerful electric lamps which at
night guard the great stockade
where the Mogok rubies are stored

many had been becoming more diff
cult recently. Democratic members

was the result of Won Hindenburg's

presidential campaign.

Once. long ago. there lived a miller
who was SO proud of his accomplished
daughter that he told the king she
could spin gold thread from straw or
silver from hemp.


So the king called the daughter to
him and demanded that she spin a
great heap of straw into gold that
night. When he went away, she wept.
for she thought her fathers foolish
boast would cost her her life


Suddenly the door opened and a
droll little dwarf entered the room.


What will you give me if I spin
the straw into gold for your" he
asked.


The maiden was so glad that she
took off her necklace, saying. Here,
l will give you this


So the manikin sat down and spun
all the straw into gold. The king was
greatly pleased the next morning, but
being a greedy man, he soon set the
millers daughter to new task.


The miller's daughter has golden
hair and pink cheeks. She is wearing
pink slip and her stockings and
shoes are gray.

And now they had gone like every
thing else.


The bakers wife said nothing. Her
lips, thin and anemic, were pressed
tight together. She wouldn't explain.
She wouldn't hold out any hope. She
wasn't sorry. She was glad. Inside
herself she was saying, Serve you

Trudchen turned slowly away. Her

They waggled this way and that under
her dwarfed and wizened little body.
They were much too long and thin
all out Of proportion, so that they
made fraulen auf and zu, with her
short plaid skirt and tam o'shanter,
look like one of those comic pen
wipers that you can make out of
matches, a scrap of old duster and
ball OF wool. Only somehow she wasn't
funny. Even the children in the gym
nasium where she went when she was
strong enough, and who hated her,
didn't laugh.


The woman with the basket stood
in the doorway and looked back at
her. She was frowning as though she
were trying to make up her mind.
Her mouth trembled. She might be
going TO smile or cry. Her face was

or later. She snapped the lid of her
basket, and tossed up her head, and
stumped out angrily.


But Trudchen knew that If she had
been any other little girl something
wonderful would have happened.


One day Trudchen's schoolmistress
had told her class the story of Robinson

Every one had burst out into mock

her teeth and sat very upright, SWal-

But in her heart she knew what she
meant. She knew it was the truth.
There was nothing terrible in being
alone with bees and flowers and even
wild beasts. But it was terrible to be
alone in world crowded with people.
They might jostle you and almost
knock you over, and yet they never
really touched you. Wherever you
went there was a barrier between you
and them, and nobody ever crossed
it even to scold. much less take you
in their arms and pet you. On the
other side they quarreled, were happy
or unhappy, but at any rate they be-
longed to one another. You were
different-it was very difficult to un-
derstand in what way, because you

You came into a shop they stopped

and looked proud and aloof. The
children in the gymnasium walked
away from you and played in another
corner. The teachers changed their
voices when they read out that you
were top OF the class. They wouldn't
hide how hard it was for them.


Sometimes it was worse than that
sometimes in winters dusk, coming

could feel how all the bitter, terrible

closed in on her. She could almos-

eyes, almost feel their hands clutch

whisperings. And she walked very
slowly, very upright, as though she
had swallowed a poker. because she

stop.


1t was like that today. The winters

The fine rain had become a deluge

The big drops danced on the pavements

they came racing down together in

great desolation was in Trudchen's

light, like unfriendly elves. Theil

VIENNA, Aug. 18.-At day
break this morning 106 anti
Semitic demonstrators had been
arrested and a score Of persons
were known to have been injured
in nightlong riots which ushered
in the world Zionist congress.


The serious stage in the rioting
was reached when the anti-Jewish
mobs rushed the police, who had
taken vigorous measures to break
up meetings held to protest
against the gathering of the Zion
lists in the ancient Hapsburg
capital.


Some Trampled to Death


or those who were injured some
were slashed with sabers. others
we're hit with stones, which flew in
all directions during the melee and
still others were trampled beneath
the feet Of policemen's horses.


In consequence of the fury which
has been aroused, the entire police
force of Vienna, aggregating 5000,
has been brought into action.


All bridges over the ordinarily
peaceful Danube leading into the
Jewish quarter of Vienna are
closely guarded.


The trouble started by organiza-
tions of youth with strong nation
alistic and anti-Senitic prejudices
who thWarting all efforts of the
police to control them were bent
upon breaking up the Zionist cob.
gress at all hazards.


The head of the Vienna police
forbade the hostile demonstrations
Nevertheless several thousand hot.
heads invaded the city and sur
rounded the hotels where the Zion
list delegates were put up. shout
ing and shrieking their hostility.


President Weizmann rejected all
suggestions for postponement of the
opening of the Congress from to-
night until tomorrow night because
of the anti-semetic demonstrations.


Order would now seem to have
been restored and the police said
today they expected no further
outbreaks.


No Jews were among those in
jured in the riots. The police have
arrested twenty-six additional
demonstrators making a total of
log under arrest for participation
in the disturbances.

England Association Wednesday

BY the Associated Press.


CAVE CITY, Ky, February 1S.-
Sand Cave Hill. torn open in the
struggle to rescue Floyd Collins from
the grip of an underground trap,
was slowly closing in again today
upon his body, without human as
sistance. Unable to release him from
the clutch of nature. the volunteers
who fought to save him joined his
family in brief and simple funeral
services at the top of the rescue
shaft, and six of his friends fulfilled
the legal formalities by announcing
his identity and accidental death.


The cement with which it was
planned to seal the boulders over
his rocky grave, did not come and
the sagging of the rescue shaft and
Its lateral tunnel indicated natures in
tention to seal him up forever. The
mud and rocks, held back for a few
days by heavy timbers in the rescue
shaft were settling back upon him.


Father Approves Decision.


Unwilling that the brave miners
should risk their lives to recover
his body, Lee Collins. his father,
agreed to leave him where he lay.
prayer, a few hymns, and the
ritual for the dead finished the story.
while movie cameras whirred and
stlll' pictures by the score were
snapped.


The best efforts of the State of
hentucky, scores of unselfish work
ers and the sympathy and prayers of
thousands had failed. DIR. William
Haziett OF Chicago, the only physi-
cian to see him in his 60-foot grave,
announced he had been reached at
least three days too late


Everett Maddox of Central City,
KY, crawled down to wash his face
and turn him face upward, and then
six OF his friends went down one by
one into the narrow tomb to identify
him for the coroner's jury, which
they composed. The last of these
was John Gerald, who risked his life
many times in the futile effort to
draw Collins out Of the natural tun-
mel before rock slide sealed off that
channel.


Then they came into Cave City,
solemnly assembled and judiciaIly
announced their verdict of death by
exposure. caused by being acciden-
tally trapped in what is commonly
called Sand Cave"


This was entered into the record
of the State Military Board, which
took testimony from all those con-
nected with the story, and the drama
ended.


Within a few hours the workers,
the officials, the soldiers, the news
paper men scattered to their homes.


The leaders who have risked their
own and their comrades lives with
out stint, when hope still lived, were
unwilling longer to ask for volun-
teers when death had won the race
Monday afternoon. Twenty-four
hours later these volunteers, with his
family, Joined in the final tribute to
his memory, and the story Of Sand Cave
was over.

train containing more than 100 pas
sengers partly left the rails early to-
day, the last two cars sideswiping and
carrying from their faStenings seven
steel pillars. A short circuit of the
third rail followed and clouds of smoke

the passengers.

of warnings that this would let in
poisonous fumes, one pane of glass
was broken. The lights in these cars
were extinguished.


Axes and crowbars were used by
firemen to pry open the doors. First
aid treatment was given the injured
at the station platform.


The accident occurred when train
was crossing a switch point at the
Thirty-fourth street station of the
West Side Interborough Subway.

MONTGOMERY, Ala, Oct. 26.
Seventeen persons are dead, fifty
injured and thousands of dollars
of property damage was done by
a tornado which swept three coun-
ties in Alabama Sunday, accord
ing to a survey of the storm area
today.


The storm, which struck first
in Pike county. swept through
Crenshaw, Bullock and Barbour
counties, laying to waste buildings
and leaving death and destruction
in its path.


Seven of the reported dead were
white persons and ten negroes.


Relief Work Under Way


Relief work was reported already
under way from Troy and other
cities in the devastated territory.


No large towns or cities were in
the path of the storm. Those who
were victims were mostly killed
when their houses collapsed under
the terrific wind, and they were
buried under the wreckage. The
damage done was largely to small
communities and outlying farms.


The heaviest loss of life was in
the territory surrounding Troy, in
Pike county, where the twister first
descended, after blowing in from
Crenshaw county. From the Troy
vicinity it ranged eastward into
Barbour and northward into Bull
lock county, where it spent its
force.


The storm left trail of wreckage
ir it's wake. Houses, fences and
outbuildings were blown to splint.
ers, trees uprooted. and terrific
downpOur of rain followed immedi-
ateIy behind the wind. This and
severe electrical storm hampered
rescue operations and prevented an
accurate check of the death toll for
several hours.

Henry pushed Jane, through the
opening, flung his arm round Ray
mond, dragged her through and
slammed the stone into place. They
were in the narrow alleyway between
the row of veronica bushes and the
terrace wall. on the spot where Mr..
George Patterson had stood listen
ing to Raymond's voice. The air, the
daylight, the mist, seemed wonderful
beyond words. Jane never again be-
held mist without remembering
that joyful lift of the heart which
came to her when the stone shut
and she drew her first long, free
breath. Henry gave her no time to
SAVIOUR the joys of freedom.


Run, run like blazes!" he shouted.


Jane ran. Once she started she
felt as if nothing would ever stop
her She heard Henry just behind
her; she heard him urging Raymond
on. and they came out of the alley
way round the end of the terrace.


Then it came.


The ground shook: there was a
long. heavy rumble that died slowly.
Then with a terrific crash two of the
stone urns along the terrace wall fell
and broke. AS the noise ebbed there
came the tinkling sound of splintered
glass falling upon stone.


Jane stopped running as if she had
been shot and reeled up against
Henry, who put his arms round her
and held her tight. Up to that very
moment the feeling of unreality, of
playing a part in a play for which
she had no responsibility whilst her
real self looked on remotely-this
feeling had dominated her. Now IT
was as if the curtain fell and she,
Jane, was left cropping amongst
events that terrified her. She trem-
bled very much, and clung to Henry,
who was at that moment the one
really safe and solid thing within
reach.


Raymond did not pause or turn her
head, but walked straight on toward
the house

ST. THOMAS, New, March 81
Pueblo Grande, Nevada's long lost
city, believed to have been the
seat of a primitive people of giant
stature who ruled Western Amer
lea centuries ago, was being grad
ually restored today by excavators
working under M. r. Harrington,
director Of the Museum of the
American Indian, who is heading
the Heye Foundation expedition into
the unknown prehistoric metropolis
in the Muddy and Virgin river val
leys, near here.


Exploration has been going on
for months. but only recently, ac-
cording to Harrington, has excava-
ton uncovered almost incontrovert-
able evidence that the once lost city
will prove to be the largest prehis-
toric ruin on the Western Hemis-
phere.


Big, sturdy round adobe build
ings, some containing as many as
twenty rooms, with hard glazed
floors, have been exoavated, reveal
ing under their CIRCULAR courtyards
the graves Of vanished race, with
the skeletons found to average over
seven feet in height.


Buried With Twins.


A woman wrapped in a feathered
blanket was found in one circular
burial place, with a set of new
born twins buried with her.


From what can be seen at pres
ent the whole planning seems to
have been circular, the houses hav.
ing walks radiating from a center
sacrificial altar or ceremonial fire
place.


In many mounds already Nun-
earthed, Harrington has. found beau
tiful shell jewelry, artistically cut
beads. and decorated pottery of
fanciful design, in addition to guam
titles of crude hunting implements
and other primitive tools.


Several sets of perfectly formed
dice, some with the corners round
ed, were discovered in. clay urns,
indicating fondness of this race
gone by for the thrill of gambling.


The area embraced by Pueblo
Grande Is eight miles wide and
extends intermittently with $50 out
groupings for thirty-five miles down
the Muddy and Virgin river valleys.


Strata upon strata, layered with
colored pottery and implements,
have been unearthed. with the
CruuSSL implements usually buried
at the greatest depths.


Had Glass Distinctions.


Evidence that class distinction
prevailed among the vanished
Nevada race was furnished when
1t was observed that some Of the
giant skeletons were found to have
far more objects Of art surround
ing them than the average burial
mound contained.


Many implements were dis
covered differing in construction
from the majority of those found
in the lost city, giving rise to the
theory that perhaps more than one
city had thrived over the same
spot.


Evidences that in more modern
times both Pueblo and Piute Indian
tribes had lived in the Muddy
and Virgin river valleysNwere also
uncovered.


Harrington said he expects to
continue his excavations until the
riddle of Pueblo Grande has been
comnleteiV solved

By the Associated Press


CHICAGO, April 10.-Richard
"Dickie" Loeb and Nathan Babe"
Leopold, millionaires' sons who a
year ago were planning the world s
perfect crime-the Staying of young
Robert Franks, after they kidnapped
him for ransom-yesterday met and
conversed for the first time since they
entered Joliet penftentiary seven
months ago to expiate their crime
in life sentences.


They were united by the Feast of
the Passover, and with Sc other Jew
ish prisoners were released for the
day from prison restraint, Loeb from
his work in the chair factory and
Leopold from weaving rattan furni-
ture.


The two youths were rather un-
nerved by the meeting, according to
guards who observed them. Hello,
Babe" said Loeb, always the leader,
and Hello, Dick" responded Leo
pold. Then they stood for time with
out speaking while other prisoners
of their faith looked on curiously,
and finally repaired to a corner
where they talked in low tones for
some time


After religious services the Jew
ish prisoners were left to themselves.
Today they went back to work, but on
next Thursday, the last day of the
Passover, they will again be allowed
to mingle. That will probably be the
last meeting of Loeb and Leopold
until the Fourth Of July. when all
the prisoners are allowed to mingle
and converse throughout the day.

VIENNA. August 15.-Negley Far
son, staff correspondent of The Star
and the Chicago Daily News, and Mrs.
t,arson on the auxiliary yawl Flame
have arrived in Vienna after an ad-
Venturous trip across Holland, Ger
many, Bavaria and Austria.


The pair followed the Rhine and
Main Rivers and then by a devious
and little known route entered the
almost forgotten Ludwig Canal by
which, in 10l locks they crossed the
Frankischer Jura Mountains.


Most Germans and Austrians have
forgotten the Ludwig Canal and look
skeptical when told that the Parsons
came this way Leaving the canal,
the Flame entered mountain tribu-
tarY of the Danube and soon was
caught in the torrential Danube itself
and whirled through it's dangerous
'strudels" or whirlpools.


t'arson accomplished the hitherto
uninterrupted feat of descending the
Danube without a pilot. He shot the
Flame through the only feasible arch
of the Regensburg Bridge. through
the rapids and through the wildly pic
turesque Wachau Gorge - but not
without finding numerous concealed
banks and bars. The craft now is un-
dergoing repairs at Vienna, while Mr..
and Mrs. Farson prepare for continu-
alton of their trip to the Black Sea.


Although the lofty mountains have
been left behind, the next stages of
the voyage promise further adven-
lures through the Hungarian plains,
the dangerous Irongate Pass and the
bandit infested swamps of the lower
Danube in lower Rumania.

The tusks of the elephant are
merely projections of the incisors of
the upper jaw and are never shed.
although they are sometimes broken
off. In other words, the tusks are part
of the elephants teeth. However, the
milk teeth, which precede the tusks,
come out at an early age. The tusks
of the elephant supply the ivory which
is so highly esteemed the world over
for ornamental purposes. Among the
Indian or Asiatic elephants only the
male has the tusks, but they are found
on both the male and female of the
African species

ALLAHABAD, Oct. S.-An extra
ordinary case Of q Hindu ascetic
who had himself buried alive has
Just been tried in the Barabank
Court.


Two men were charged with abet-
ting his suicide. Their reply was
that the ascetic voluntarily de-
scended into a grave which they
had dug. and they admitted filling
in the earth. While this process
was in progress they said the man
chanted religious songs.


At the same time they said they
were only acting on the instruc-
tons of the man, because they
were his disciples and bound to
obey his commands.


Defense pleaded that the holy
man had not committed suicide, but
had merely performed the religious
rite of "samadhi," that is, being
buried alive whilst in a state of
suspended animation.


The court accepted this defense
and the prisoners were set free.

NEW YORK, April 14.-Mrs. Bessie
Katz, who last December killed her
twin babies by throwing them from
third-story window of her home,
was found dead last night in a gas
filled apartment. Dependency over
the death of the children was be-
lieved to have caused the suicide.


On December Mrs. Katz became
deranged and threw her three weeks
old twin boys from her window and
jumped out after them. One of the
children was killed almost instantly
and the other died in a few hours.
Mrs. Katz received broken arm and
internal injuries. Physicians said the
shock of her action had restored her
mind to normal, and on recommends
ton of the district attorneys Office
the charge of homicide against her
was dismissed.

marine signal receivers may deter
mine their distance from the light
vessel with accuracy.

80 seconds, groups Of four dashes for
60 seconds and then is silent for 80
seconds. The submarine oscillator
sounds three groups of six blasts
every 90 seconds, thus: Six blasts of
one second each, 2 seconds silent;
six blasts of one second each, 81 sec
onds silent; silence between blasts in
group, 3.5 seconds. In each reception
Of the characteristics of the signals
the first dash of the radio fog signal
and the first blast of the oscillator
are sounded simultaneously; the diff
ference in time in seconds between
the reception of the dash and the
blast multiplied by 1000 gives the
distance in yards separating the OBJ
serving vessel from the light vessel.

BALTIMORE, December THE
holiday volume of trade this year will
break all previous records, according
to merchants Buying began earlier
than usual and is now in full swing.
Initial orders placed by retail dealers
were larger than they had been for
several years, but despite this fact re-
peat orders have been numerous and
restocking continues brisk.


About the only complaint heard Is
that the mild weather has retarded
buying of seasonable goods. There
is seasonal slowing down in wholesale
lines. but dealers report sales have
been large and that they are rounding
out one Of the best years they ever
realized.


Outlook for 1925 is promising.

CHICAGO. June 13.-Chicago gang
land and Chicago policemen met today

shot to death, another probably
fatally wounded, one gangster was
killed and his two companions cap

and spectacular pistol battles in the
city's history.


Tonight 5000 Chicago policemen
were securing the city in what Chief
of Police Morgan A. Collins described
as a relentless and merciless drive on
gangland and scores of suspects had
been taken into custody.


The police and the gangsters met on
the southwest side and the pistol bat
tie followed 60-mile-an-hour auto
mobile chase which ended when the
gangsters' car was wrecked and they
tumbled from their machine with
blazing guns.


Gets Three Gangsters.


The hero Of the battle was William
Sweeney, young policeman, who
escaped the fusillade of bullets that
wounded or killed his three comrades,
and then single handed killed one of
the ;;angsters and caught the two
others after wounding them.


True to the gangland code, the
captured gunmen remained stolidly
silent through hours of questioning,
but tonight the police were satisfied
that the battle was the aftermath Of
a trip by the gangsters to avenge the
death of Angelo Genna, gang leader.
slain a few weeks ago. Michael
Genna, his brother, was the gangster
shot and killed today.


Half an hour before Genna and his
men began their savage battle with
the detective squad, six gunmen tried
to assassinate an unidentified motor
list several miles from the scene of
the fight. They emptied sawed-of
shotguns and pistols at the car but
missed the occupant. The police be-
lieve that Genna and his companions
were In that ambuscade and believed
that they had been detected by the
police and decided to shoot it out.


Pole Ends Flight.


The police auto met the gangsters
machine racing over a southwest side
boulevard and gave chase. The race
ended after a two-mile run at break
neck speed when the gangsters' car
crashed into a corner light pole. The
three gangSterS leaped from their car
as the police car drew up a few feet
away and the four detectives tumbled
out. A shotgun volley met them.
Patrolman Harold Olson, driver of the
police car was dropped in his tracks,
and moment later Patrolman
Charles Walsh also fell fatally
wounded.


The two policemen left advanced
with blazing pistols until Sergt.
Michael Conway collapsed, shot
through the chest and probably
fatally wounded.


Then the gangsters took to their
heels. Patrolman Sweeney, who was
uninjured started in pursuit Of
Michael Genna. Genna turned as the
policeman advanced and aimed his
shotgun directly at the officer, but
the hammer clicked harmlessly. Then
Genna threw the gun away and ran.
the policeman in pursuit and firing at
every step. AS Genna started into
the basement of a building a block
away, Sweeney shot him dead.


Leaving Genna, the patrolman sped
in pursuit Of the other two gunmen
who had boarded a street car.

Cattle in southwest Virginia are be-
ing marketed earlier than usual this
year, according to the United States
Bureau of Agricultural Economics.
The early movement is due largely
to the severe drought conditions which
have prevailed throughout the south
ern Appalachian region and seriously
affected pastures and crops. Fortu-
nately for producers market prices
nave been somewhat higher than last
year and this may account in part
for the earlier shipping.


The bureaus recent study of cattle
marketing problems in southwest Nir-
ginia revealed that the best prices
for the grass-finished cattle of this
section are usually obtained in July
and August. 1t appears that during
these months in normal times these
cattle meet less competition from cat
tie of similar grade produced else
where.


Later in the season they are forced
into competition with hordes of West
ern grass cattle which come on the
market in the Fall months.

who walked out yesterday in pro-
test against compulsory military
and physical training, today de-

classes until their demands are
met by the faculty.

been dismissed for alleged "cut-

sidetrack the strikers from their
determination to remain out.


Error In Record.

declared that three of the students
had been reinstated following dis
covery of an error in the at
tendance records.

assembled students. The faculty
adviser returned to the faculty con.
ference, room and reported the re-
ception OF the letter.


Another communication was
drafted. and further concessions
made in the reinstatement of the
remaining two dismissed pupils.
This. likewise, was received with
Kisses.


New Demands Made


New demands were made by the
strike leaders today. Briefly, they
are:


1student representation on the
faculty.


2-Cutting down the reserve Off
GERS training course from three to
two years, with the idea of eventu-
ally eliminating military training.


3-Reducing physical training
from four years to three.

NEW YORK, January 10.-Two attor-
neys, representing Edwin w. Jacobs,
who recently brought suit against Cyrus
Fl. Mccormick. son OF the inventor OF
the harvester, for alienation OF Mrs.
Jacobs affections, yesterday requested
Federal Judge Augustus n. Hand to
compel two other attorneys, who rep
resented Jacobs in bringing the suit, to
discontinue the action.


Although il had been reported that
the suit had been settled out of court,
Jacobs original attorneys refused TO
discontinue the action, alleging that
they had not received their fee from
Jacobs. They said they believed Jacobs
had received monetary settlement
without their knowledge.


Details of the settlement of the suit,
which was for $500, 900. were not re-
vealed at the hearing, but Matthews
and Rothwell, present attorneys for
Jacobs, said the latter had received
nothing.


Burger & Burger. former attorneys
for Jacobs, asked for payment of 81, 500
fees for services rendered. and requested
permission to tell the court of the serv-
les performed. Mr.. Matthews objected.
however. on the ground that this would
violate the confidence of his client and
that matters would be brought out
which were not privileged. Jacobs, Mr..
Matthews said, was not financially able
to pay a heavy fee.


Judge Hand ruled that Burger & Bur
ger might submit an affidavit OF serv-
ices performed and that he would then
render a decision.

ROME, January 24-Even optimists
at the Vatican no longer believe the
French embassy to the Holy See can
be saved, either by Aristide Brands
eloquence or the French Senate's
calmer viewpoint


While the unclerical press here unt-
versally deplores the rupture between
Rome and France, the Vatican is ex-
tremely reserved. High prelates who
allow themselves guarded opinion
do not agree as TO the rultIre's real
import. Those more Immediately in
touch with the papal secretar.at 81
state pronounce it disastrous to
French Catholic interests" but prel-
ates closely connected with French
religious views here think otherwise.


Neglected by Diplomats.


These explain that during the snort
period when France resumed dtplo-
matte relations with the Holy See
French Catholic interests were
neglected by the very diplomats sent
to Rome to protect them These
diplomats were quite beyond their
depth in dealing with the abated
policy OF the Vatican and, denlorably
ignorant of the countless byways
that make network through fue
vast Catholic organization. !rcre apt
TO treat their posts as q social rathe.
than religious undertaking.


When no embassy existed Frances
Catholic emissaries to the Pope were
the competent heads Of ecclesiastical
colleges and religious homes. who
worked the same system used by
United States Catholics today. The
results were infinitely more favorable
to real spiritual interests than when
the embassy was revived


Naturally, those favoring the en-
bassy deplore the danger to Frances
civil concord, and hint darkly of a
terrible revenge in the near future.
This, they suggest, will come from
the population of Alsace-LoFraine,
which already is irritated over
Frances refusal to allow them
separate concord to replace the one
they enjoyed under German rule.


Thus, say these gloomy prophets,
q purely religious problem soon will

BUENOS AIRES, April 17.-Presi.
dent d'Alvear yesterday issued a de.
cree prohibiting importation into Ar
gentina of fruits and vegetables from
countries where the Mediterranean
fruit fly exists. Exception is made in
the decree to lemons, bananas, cocoa
nuts and pineapples. The countries
specified in the decree are Cuba, Italy,
Spain, Brazil, South Africa, Australia
and New Zealand.


The decree was issued after a. visit
here of the United States Federal
Horticultural Board, who advised the
minister of agriculture that should
the fruit fly pest become established
in Argentina it would cause the
United States to bar out Argentine
fruits.

HOBOKEN, N. j., Sept. 1S.-
With threats still rumbling in Irish
republican circles to stage another
demonstration against a party of
visiting Free State opponents,
three men and two women were
arraigned in court today and con-
victed as alleged members of the
mob which yesterday attacked
General Richard Mulcahy, former
commander Of the Irish Free State
army.


Four of the prisoners, including
two women, were released with
suspended sentences for disorderly
conduct. Patrick keenan, was
ordered held for the grand jury
for atrocious assault and battery
but released on his own recog-
nizance.


General Mulcahy was accom-.
panied by Thomas johnson, labor
leader OF the Dali, and Michael
Hayes, another Dali member. They
arrived on the steamship President
Roosevelt to attend the Interpar-
liamentary Congress in Washington.
A small welcoming committee which
was at the pier to greet the Free
Skaters was dispersed when the
mob, composed largely Of women,
began hurting sticks. tomatoes,
eggs and epithets as the visitors
walked down the gangplank.


Police Rescue MuIcahy


MuIcahy was cursed and beaten
and showered with eggs and to-
matoes, but stood his ground until
a group OF police rescued him.


Members OF the mob carried ban
ners with inscriptions derogatory
to Mulcahy and the Free State.


"Mulcahy - the murderer Of
Seventy-seven," said one. George
Washington and Eamonn de Valera
Benedict Arnold and Richard
Mulcahy," said another. "Mulcahy,
murderer; Mulcahy, perjuror; Null
cahy, traitor said a third.


In the melee someone pinned
small Union Jack on Mulcahy's
coat lapel.


Police Reserves Called


During the excitement one of the
pier police turned in a riot call.
With the police who answered came
a crowd Of some $500 persons to
find out what the trouble was
about.


The attackers were finally driven
off and Mulcahy, the two Dali
members and some of the welcom-
ing committee were assembled and
taken to a taxicab in police escort
to the Fourteenth street ferry,
which took them to Manhattan.


Police said some women who were
at the pier, but whom they could
not connect directly with the at
tack on the Free Skaters told them
the pier demonstration was only
a part of the series of demonstra-
tons that had been planned.

CAMBRIDGE, Mass, July 23.-Two
men We're killed, three more received
injuries which are believed will prove
fatal, three others seriously injured
and two escaped after the automobile
in which they had been speeding
through this city last night crashed
into an iron trolley pole as the driver
sought to escape a pursuing police
patrol.


The dead are Charles Baylis and
Oscar Williams, both of Cambridge.
Three of their companions were taken
to the Cambridge city hospital, where
their names were placed on the danger
list, while two others are expected to
recover.


The police said they had received
numerous complaints during the eve
ming that an automobile loaded with
young men was speeding through the
streets. A policeman was nearly run
down when he stepped into the street
to hail the car.


He notified headquarters and
patrol wagon was sent in pursuit. The
police machine sighted the speeding
car. which, officers said. was filed with
yelling men, and attempted to over
haul it, but was losing ground when
the fleeing car swerved into the pole.
The officers saw two of its occupants
run away.

BOSTON, February 2S.-An earth
quake at 9:25 tonight rocked all New
England. No casualties were re-
ported. but slight damage was done In
many localities. The lights in the
Ward Baking Co. in Cambridge,
Mass, went out when the building
was moved several inches, 1t was re-
ported In dozens of theaters, panics
were narrowly averted. Several audi
ences left the buildings. From homes
and offices people poured into the
streets when the trembling began. A
minute later all telephone offices
were swamped by thousands of ex-
cited subscribers demanding infor-
nation.


The shock played many pranks.
Bells rang in church steeples, books
toppled from shelves and pictures
from walls doors slammed and win
dows ratified Plastering fell in
rooms and in scattered points tele-
phone and electric wires were
snapped.


Buildings Are Shaken.


NEW YORK, February 2S.-An
earth shock of two minutes duration
was felt in New York City and its
suburbs this evening. Shocks also
were reported from upstate counties
in New York as far west as Syracuse
and throughout New England.


In Manhattan, New York's sky
scraper borough, the shock was plain
ly felt by late workers in the great
office buildings. The New York World
building on Park Row was shaken.


The seismograph reports insisted
that the quake was only "a slight
earth tremor," but to millions of peo-
pie it was an exciting event and
newspaper offices were flooded with
queries.


In Syracuse, business buildings
waved, and frightened occupants
rushed into the streets.

The display of tulips around the
Capitol seems to grow more wonder
full every year. This year II is a
trumpet blast in color, delightfully."-
echoed in gardens all over the city.
Whether it is improvements in the
breeding of tulips, or merely the ever
swelling numbers of the gay armies
of these flowers, they are certainly
the victory parade of Washington S
Spring.


1t is strange to think that the tulip
does not really belong to us, so much
part of our gardens has it grown,
but 1t comes to us from over the
water. Not even Holland can boast
the paternity, for tulips did not reach
that country till about 1900. They
came originally from Asia Minor and
Persia, and like the lilac and horse
chestnut, were first brought to Eu-
rope by the Austrian Ambassador at
Constantinople.


The Turks seemed to have pre-
ferred the red and yellow tulips with
narrow petals, and at first this kind
was the only sort grown, though the
round faced Dutchman selected by
preference the round -petalled types.
Soon, however. the popular taste in
tulips grew sophisticated and craved
'o-AOey' ia MS lIic SEcdl
mania" of 1880, when bulbs were
more precious than the precious
metals and there was tulip specula-
mania" of 1880, when bulbs were
those that produced strange new
howers-white-g ground petals with
various gorgeous splashes, and all the
shades of mauve. lilac, rose, purple,
and even the famous black tulips.
The marvellous Jagged kind, called
Parrot" was early developed by
horticulturalists and sold for hun
dreds of dollars a bulb.


Today the despised simple red and
yellow tulips have returned to favor.
They form the flower of those bright
armies that now besiege the Capitol
with f1uttering banners.


Nowadays there are tulips for every
taste-doubles and parrots and
bizarres for those who love fantastic
shapes, Darwins for those who like
pastel colors, and the plain old fash
ioned cottage tulips for the simple of
heart who like the strong gay colors
and well known forms

SYDNEY. Nova Scotia, June 10
The British Empire Steel Corporation
store at Caledonia No. 4. a suburb of
Glace Bay, was burned to the ground
early today. The building which was
two stories In height and of wood
construction, had been raided and
partially looted last night by striking
coal miners.


The fire started at 2 o'clock and
the spectacular blaze lighted up the
mining village for the first time since
strike pickets drove maintenance men
from the new Waterford power plant
a week ago and put the electric light
service out of commission. The build
ing houses a general store, butcher
shop and warehouse.


The Glace Bay fire department was
on the scene, but devoted its energies
to saving nearby buildings.

MURPHYsBORO, H.. March 90
Southern Illinois presented a funereal

With the cessation of first frenzied

dotted with prosperous cities and

CHICAGO. October 2S.-Under
blanket of snow, the Midwest and
Rocky Mountain region today faced
the prospect of continued low tenn
peratures, with cold wave in south
ern Missouri, Illinois and Indiana.


The white covering, which broke
records in Milwaukee and endangered
the unharvested sugar beet crop in
Colorado, was nearly 10 inches thick
at Helena, Mont, and a half foot or
more in many sections of Iowa.


Accompanying the snowfall were
dropping temperatures, reaching 2
degrees above at Havre, Mont, the
coldest spot in the country yesterday,
and lowering around the freezing
mark in the corn belt region.


Kansas expected from Is to 20 de
grees above zero today and Omaha
looked for 90 degrees.


The low temperatures of northeast
ern Colorado caused business men and
school children to turn out in aiding
farmers efforts to save the beet crop,
valued at 100000.


Some reaction will set in tomorrow,
1t was forecast, in the northern Rocky
Mountain region and northwestern
plains area, moving eastward to the
western great lake region.


Chicago had relief from the flying
flakes today, but fresh northwesterly
winds and dropping mercury preserved
the inches of snow that fell last night.

brother, John, having been killed

Mill.

mas River early today. Mrs. Ben
son left her home yesterday morn

passing Western Maryland Railway
train saw the body in the water
about a mile below Piedmont and
notified the authorities. She Is
survived by her husband and one
son, Harmon.

George Gill, %, senior law student at
Loyola University. New Orleans, was
held today in connection with the
mysterious disappearance of Robert
(Bob) Read. Centenary College senior,
athlete and gridiron star, whom he
confessed Staying Wednesday night at
Pleasureville, bathing resort near
here, ito protect the honor of his
home"


Read was last seen Wednesday
night. when he engaged a row boat
at Pleasureville. Following Gill's con-
fession. search was made for Read g
body in Old River.


Sheriff Hughes said last night that
Gill had admitted killing the young
Centenary senior. but had intended
only Ito thrash him for insistent and
annoying attentions to Mrs. GILL;"


According to the confession. Read
demanded that Mrs. Gill meet him at
Pleasureville. threatening her If she
refused. She told her husband of
Reads threats and he accompanied
her to the resort, intending to thrash
Read. Gill said Read attacked him
and, struggling, they fell into the
water.


Beat Head Against Boat.


Read was trying to kill him, Gill
said, and to save himself he dashed
Reads head against the rowboat
which Read had rented and which
was near them in the water.


Read became unconscious, the pris-
oner Is quoted as saying, and he let
the body sink into the water.


He then climbed into Reads boat
and padded to shore, he and his wife
leaving for the home of relatives
without making a report of the affair
to any one.


Gill's arrest followed after a por-
ton of the night. and the following
day was spent in fruitless search for
Read


Police received information that
Mrs. Gill made several telephone calls
to Read during Wednesday and that
Gill was at her side during each con-
versation with the missing collegian.


This Gill denied. He said that while
Mrs. Gill talked to Read on the tele-
phone "Wednesday, that Read made
the calls and was demanding that she
keep her appointment at Pleasureville
with him. Mrs. Gill corroborated her
husbands version of the affair and
was released, pending further inquiry.

Dear Bill: Here are q few
historic facts about August,
named for the Roman Emperor
Augustine. In Rome, during
tie days of the republic, the
year began with March, and
August was the sixth month,
as its name, Sextilis, indicates.
But after Julius Caesar made
his reforms in the calendar
August became the eighth
month. This alone would not
have led to its remaining, but
Caesar rechristined the month
Of July for himself and his sue
cessor Augustus desired q like
honor for himself. Requested
to make his choice, he took his
lucky month";" the month in
which he had been elected con-
sui, had three times celebrated
q triumph, and had completed
the conquest of Egypt. But
here difficulty arose. July
had thirty-one days and the
newly named month had but
thirty; thus Julius was yet
more honored than Augustus. !
Since this was not to be
thought of, a day was taken
from February, already the
least of the months, and given
to August. TUXEDO.

THE other day Clarence Gilbert, air

night in a binding snowstorm, his plane
loaded with mail, bound for Omaha

lonely flight were the beacons at occa-
sional emergency air mail fields and the

forced to Jump to avoid death in crash.

was killed in the fall.

schedule, another pilot, r. G.. Page, took
off while the storm still ragged, and in
the early dawn located the wreckage of
Gilberts plane


Page fought his way to the nearest
farm house, sent message 20 his chief,
fought his way back to Gilbert's wrecked
plane. loaded the delayed mailbagS into
his own plane. leaving the farmers 10
scour the countryside for Gilbert's body
and rushed the mail TO Omaha


All of which illustrates dramatically the
heroiSm, the high sense of duty and effici-
ency. and the spirit of the United States
air mail service No army ever displayed
more courage than this peacetime force,
which daily fights the elements day and
night to get the air mail there on time.

Lotteries are conducted in Cuba
regularly. The public knows
beforehand all about them, how

In the days Of the Honduras and

LOTTERY!


Suppose you buy a ticket. You
are told that if you happen to
strike a winning combination, you
will draw down $4,000. Some
pools promise more than that.
But, when you attempt to cash
in your winning ticket, the agent
calmly informs you that so many
were the winners that your share
is a mere pittance, possibly $25

Do you KNOW ANYBODY who

Ban Johnson, president of the
American league, has repeatedly
tried to obtain laws prohibiting
baseball pools. He succeeded i'll
getting Illinois to adopt his sug-
gestion, but generally around the
country baseball pools are per-
mitted openly, tickets selling at
drug stores, billiard halls and
newsstands, not to mention blind
pigs, shoe shine parlors and what
not. Ban did want a Federal law,
but failed to get it for some
reason not known to this writer


With the baseball season at
hand, get ready to see the base
ball lotteries in action, with the
suckers falling into line like
trained sheep.


This writer's advice,-which
won't be followed, naturallyI-,is
for everybody to turn down the
lottery ticket. Blow your dough
on the gals or buy bootleg liquor.
Get some value for your money,
anyway, which is more than
you'll get by seeking the "soft
money" in the baseball pools now
being conducted in this country.

BRUSSELS, July 1.-THE Belgian
government has agreed with the
French and British for the early
evacuation of Duesseldorf, Duisburg
and Ruhrort, simultaneous with the
evacuation of other places in the
Ruhr.


Recent dispatches have said prepa-
rations were being completed for the
allied evacuation of the Ruhr not
later than August 16, the date fixed
by the London agreement of 1924,
which put the Dawes plan into effect.
Already a number of small towns in
the Ruhr have been evacuated. Essen
and Bochum are to be freed soon.
Dusseldorf, Duisburg and Ruhrort
are so-called sanctions cities" and
their evacuation was made conditional
by the London agreement upon Ger
many's fulfillment of her Dawes plan
obligations.


Although some allied troops already
have been withdrawn from the Ruhr
and other Withdrawals are continuing
every day, political police will remain
until August 16 as an indication that
the occupation technically continues
to the date specified by the London
agreement,

atty rubs shoulders with "gillies,''

of the larger fish in the lake went

but thOusa ndS of small fry were left

basin.

boundary separating Turkey from

province Immediately to the south.

dominantly Arab, and she promises

line 10 the south of Mosul.

Great Britain to accept the proposal,

Mosul oil field vested in an all
British company.

origin in the establishment of the

potamia, sponsored by Great Britain.

great meteorological station which is
being built on a Danish island for
constant wireless communication with
all stations on the Northern Henri
sphere. Arrangements have been made

atmospheric conditions.

meteorologists find the weather is
favorable the flight will start Two

cessive governments since the war

police. They carried several banners.

I'VE demand unrestricted immigration

stop persecution of foreign born" !"

escorted to the Hotel Pennsylvania,
where they will remain until going
to Washington for the conference
which opens Thursday.

of the British Exchequer, heading the
English delegation, was delayed and
will arrive on the Majestic tomorrow.

strips Lay the strips in a pile, one
above the other. Cut them into
squares and pile up again. Press
down with the hand and roll out thin.
Cut into strips and then in squares
and roll out again. Repeat this sew
eral times and roll thin. Always roll
in the direction from you. This pas
try is good for pies, for dessert and
also for oyster and chicken pates.

DUBLIN. Feb. 3.-The Lady Dud-
ley Nursing Association began send
ing oil stoves and oil to the famine
districts Of West Ireland today.
Miss Jebb. OF the London "save the
children fund" has arrived here and
will at once open relief centers for
the stricken people.


The Irish Free State is purchas.
ing old railroad ties and selling
them for a pittance to the sufferers
for fuel. The government also is
supplying nets for fisherman who
lost their own during the recent
gales. But even with these nets
the catches are very small.


Depressing reports come from
Galway. Travellers tell of shoeless
children with hunger indelibly inn
printed on their thin faces: mothers
with babes at their breasts and
showing signs of under-nourish-
ment; and depressed men. all un
stone and sod rooted novels.


Death has not made any great
inroads Of these people but many
would welcome death, travellers
said, rather than continue to endure
the daily pangs Of hunger and suf'
fering from the cold.


One tiny hut houses a family OF
seven in two rooms. All day long
they crouch about heap of smould-
ering wet. peat which gives off so
little heat 1t could be picked up
from the hearth.


Another cabin of two rooms holds
a family of twelve who sleep In
two beds and on the flagstones OF
the hearth. Even the hovel-like
homes of those people appear to
add to their discomfort. for the
rainsoaked sod roofs and stone
walls hold moisture until the sun
dries it out.


The daily fare in the famine dis
tricts consists of tea and bread for
breakfast, tea and bread at mid
day, in the evening dry. unbuttered
bread Some families have small
store of bedwarfed potatoes which
represents their years labor. These
potatoes are harbored closely and
are rationed carefully.

NEW YORK, June 30.-Miss
Mary X. Browne of Santa Monica,
Cal, former national women's
tennis champion and the present
second ranking player in the coun-
try, has reached here from the
Pacific coast. Miss Browne will
rest this week from her transcon-
tinentaI trip and on Monday will
make her first tournament appear
ance in the East, at Providence,
where she will compete for the
women's Rhode Island clay court
championship at the Agawam
Hunt Club.


Miss Browne, who was runner-up
for the national golf championship
last year, left her clubs behind and
intends to devote herself solely to
tennis. She will make another bid
for the national championship and
is expected to be a member of the
women's international team that
will play the British for the
Wightman Cup at Forest Hills in
August.

BALTIMORE. Md, August A.
The fortieth anniversary of the
first commercially operated electric
street car line in America will be
observed here next week by the
United Railways and Electric Co,
which controls what was the pre-
mier electric railway system.


The Baltimore Union Passenger
Railway was the first electric line
which operated by means of third
rail and the system was tried out
August 10, 1885. Overhead wiring
was used on portions of the line
after 1t was found that the exposed
third rail shocked horses and other
animals passing over crossings.


The rail was not protected as are
the third rails on many present
day systems.
